script.opening: (You play Kirsty, Daniel's support worker; Daniel can be heard moaning in the background.) "Hiya, it's about Daniel, he's 24, he's got a learning disability and he's autistic. He's been really difficult this past week — hitting himself, won't eat properly, up all night, more agitated than usual. We think it's just his autism playing up, a behaviour thing. We don't really need to examine him or anything, he hates that — maybe just something to calm him down?"

facts.text: Uses a few words and Makaton signs, loves trains and his tablet, usually calm and smiley, eats well (likes soft foods and crisps), sleeps 10pm–7am. Lives in a supported living house with 24-hour staff.

For seven days: hitting the right side of his face and jaw with his hand, pushing food away — he will only take yoghurt and drinks through a straw — up most of the night, crying. "He's never done the face-hitting before."

facts.topic: On video (if asked to show him)
facts.text: Daniel holds the right side of his jaw and rocks. If asked to look closely: his right cheek looks a bit puffy compared with the left. You cannot see inside his mouth.

Temperature: "He felt warm last night; we didn't check." Bowels opened yesterday, normal. Passing urine normally. No cough, no vomiting, no rash, no ear-pulling. No falls or injuries that you know of.
"He hasn't seen a dentist in years — he won't let anyone near his mouth. Teeth brushing is a battle."
No regular medicines. No allergies. Has a hospital passport. Has not had an annual health check for two years.
Two staff off sick; you have done three night shifts in a row. You are tired and the house manager suggested "asking the GP for something".

Kind but tired and a bit stuck in "it's his behaviour". If the doctor suggests he might be in pain, think about it and agree: "Actually... he does keep going for that side of his face." Be helpful once the doctor explains, and share what calms Daniel (quiet room, his tablet, his favourite worker Joe). Raise the practical problem that he will not tolerate examination — respond well to suggestions of adjustments.

ice.ideas: "It's just his autism playing up — a behaviour thing."
ice.concerns: Daniel hurting himself, and the staff struggling to cope.
ice.expectations: "Something to calm him down." You will support an assessment if it is planned around Daniel's needs.

cues: "He's never done the face-hitting before." — say when describing the change.
"He keeps going for the right side of his face." — say if asked where he hits himself.
"He won't let anyone near his mouth." — say if teeth or examination come up.

checkpoints.text: Recognises DIAGNOSTIC OVERSHADOWING: a CHANGE in behaviour (self-injury, off food, not sleeping, agitation) in a person with learning disability/autism who cannot easily report symptoms is likely a sign of untreated PHYSICAL ILLNESS or PAIN — NOT "just their autism/behaviour" — and does NOT simply sedate

Actively seeks a PHYSICAL CAUSE: notes the jaw-holding/off-food and considers dental abscess/pain, ear/throat, constipation, urinary infection, etc., and plans to assess/examine for it (and treat the cause) rather than attributing it to behaviour

Makes REASONABLE ADJUSTMENTS (Equality Act): extra time/longer appointment, calm quiet approach, involving someone who knows his baseline and communication/pain cues, gentle/desensitised examination, hospital passport/communication tools, and pain-assessment tools for non-verbal patients — treating "he hates being examined" as a reason to ADJUST, not skip
Involves those who know his NORMAL communication and pain behaviours, and uses collateral history to interpret the change — recognising the change-from-baseline as the key signal
Situates it in the health-INEQUALITY context: this group has poorer access and avoidable premature mortality; ensures the annual health check and ongoing equitable care, and advocates for Daniel
Gently CHALLENGES the overshadowing and advocates for Daniel, supporting the (well-meaning, possibly fatigued) worker without colluding with "just calm him down"
Centres Daniel as the patient — his dignity, distress and right to have his pain taken seriously — and communicates in a way that includes him as far as possible

Safety-nets and follows up: the physical-cause assessment (urgent dental/pain review as indicated), treating the cause, reasonable adjustments documented, baseline-knowledgeable carers involved, the annual health check, and review — not sedation of unexplained distress

worked.txt: "Thank you for ringing about Daniel. Can I offer a different way of looking at this? When someone who finds it hard to tell us they’re in pain suddenly changes — hitting himself, off his food, not sleeping — that’s very often his way of saying something HURTS, not just ‘his autism’. New behaviour like this, I always treat as a possible sign of physical illness until we’ve checked. It’s too easy, and sadly too common, to put it down to the disability and miss something treatable."

"You said he’s holding his jaw and won’t eat — that makes me think of his teeth or mouth, maybe an abscess, which is really painful. Or it could be his ears, his tummy (constipation’s common), or a water infection. So rather than calm him down, I want to find what’s hurting and treat THAT — which is what will actually settle him."

"I know he hates being examined — so let’s do it his way. We’ll take extra time, keep it calm and quiet, have you or whoever knows him best there, go gently, and use his hospital passport if he has one. ‘He hates it’ is a reason for us to adapt, not to skip checking him — he deserves the same thorough look anyone else would get."
"You know his normal better than anyone — what’s different this week, how he usually shows pain, what’s changed with his eating and sleep. That’s gold for me. Let’s use it to work out what’s wrong."

"People with a learning disability too often have pain and illness missed because it’s blamed on their condition, and they come to harm because of it. I don’t want that for Daniel. So we check him properly, and I’ll make sure he’s had his annual health check and is getting everything he’s entitled to."

"So: let’s get him assessed today with those adjustments — likely a dental review urgently if it’s his mouth — and treat whatever’s causing the pain. If he becomes very unwell, feverish, won’t drink, or the distress escalates, contact us/again same-day. We’re not going to sedate Daniel for something that’s hurting him — we’re going to find it and fix it."

f.learning: A CHANGE in behaviour (self-injury, off food, not sleeping, agitation) in a person with learning disability/autism who cannot easily report symptoms is very often a sign of untreated PHYSICAL ILLNESS or PAIN — not "just their autism/behaviour". Attributing it to the disability and missing the physical cause is DIAGNOSTIC OVERSHADOWING, a major cause of avoidable harm and premature death in this group, so new behaviour change must trigger a search for a physical cause/pain (here, jaw-holding and off-food suggest a dental abscess; also consider ear/throat, constipation, urinary infection) and treatment of the cause rather than sedation. People with learning disability/autism are entitled to REASONABLE ADJUSTMENTS (Equality Act 2010) — extra time, a calm approach, involving those who know their baseline and pain cues, gentle/desensitised examination, hospital passports and non-verbal pain-assessment tools — so "he hates being examined" is a reason to ADJUST, not to skip assessment. The examinable hidden agenda is the well-meaning-but-harmful overshadowing assumption (and possible carer fatigue); gently challenge it and advocate for Daniel, centre him as the patient, situate it in the health-inequality context (poorer access/outcomes, the annual health check), and find-and-fix the cause.

knowledge.guideline: Equality Act 2010 (reasonable adjustments) · Mental Capacity Act 2005 · NICE NG11 (challenging behaviour and learning disabilities, 2015) · NHS England STOMP programme · LeDeR programme · Accessible Information Standard
knowledge.summary: New self-injury, poor eating and poor sleep in a young man who cannot easily report pain is a physical problem until proved otherwise. Jaw-holding points to dental pain. Assess him in person with reasonable adjustments, find and treat the cause, and do not sedate distress.

points.t: Attributing new symptoms to the learning disability or autism rather than looking for a cause. LeDeR reviews of deaths of people with a learning disability and autistic people repeatedly identify it as a contributor to avoidable harm.

NICE NG11: when behaviour that challenges develops or changes, assess for physical health problems, including pain, and consider dental problems, constipation, infection and sensory problems. Here jaw-holding plus poor eating makes dental pain or abscess the leading possibility.

NICE NG11 advises considering antipsychotic medication for behaviour that challenges only when psychological and other interventions have not helped or the risk is severe, and reviewing it closely. NHS England’s STOMP programme aims to stop inappropriate psychotropic prescribing in this group.

points.h: Reasonable adjustments are a legal duty
points.t: Equality Act 2010: longer or quieter appointments, the first or last slot, a familiar supporter present, step-by-step explanation, desensitised examination and pain-assessment tools such as DisDAT. The Accessible Information Standard requires communication needs to be recorded and met. “He hates being examined” means adapt, not omit.

Mental Capacity Act 2005: assume Daniel has capacity, give him every practicable support to decide, and assess decision-specifically. A support worker cannot consent for him. If he lacks capacity for the examination or treatment, act in his best interests, consult those who know him, and choose the least restrictive option.

People on the GP learning disability register are offered an annual health check from age 14, with a health action plan. Use this contact to check he is on the register, flag his reasonable adjustments and book the check.

dg.d: Greeted Daniel directly, then used an open question about what had changed from his usual self.
Staffing pressures, sleepless nights for carers, his routine and how he usually communicates pain.
Same-day face-to-face examination with adjustments: mouth and teeth, ears, abdomen, temperature; urine if feasible; pain-assessment tool.
Dental pain or abscess first; ear or throat infection, constipation, urinary infection, injury; mood or environmental change only after physical causes.
Asked about facial swelling, fever, trismus, swallowing, breathing and fluid intake.
Probable dental pain causing behaviour change, and named diagnostic overshadowing kindly.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: No sedation; analgesia now; urgent dental care with adjustments; best-interests process if he lacks capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005).
Learning disability register, reasonable adjustments recorded, hospital passport used, annual health check booked.
Same-day review; 999 or A&E for swelling, fever, trismus, swallowing or breathing difficulty, or not drinking.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the face-hitting, jaw-holding and stopping eating, and pursued each.
The worker’s belief it was behaviour, fatigue and difficulty examining him, and the request for calming medication.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Daniel hurting himself, and the staff struggling to cope — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Lee. Thank you for calling. Can I say hello to Daniel first? Hello Daniel — I’m a doctor. I can see you’re upset. I’m going to talk with your support worker and try to help.
model.why: Centres Daniel as the patient from the first sentence

model.text: He’s not really going to answer you, doctor. Like I said, it’s his autism playing up. We just wondered about something to calm him down.
I understand — it’s been a hard week for everyone. I’d like to hear exactly what’s changed, because working out why is how we help him settle. Then we’ll agree what to do. Is that okay?
model.why: Sets an agenda that does not accept the premise

model.text: Yeah, fine.
Tell me about Daniel when he’s his usual self. What’s different this week?
model.why: Establishes baseline so the change becomes the key finding

model.text: Normally he’s settled, likes his routine. This week he’s been hitting himself, not eating properly, up all night. More agitated than we’ve seen for a long time.
That’s a real change. Where on himself is he hitting — is it one particular place?
model.why: Localises self-injury, which often points to the site of pain

model.text: Now you say it… it’s mostly the side of his face. And he keeps holding his jaw.
That’s really important. When he tries to eat, what happens?
model.why: Follows the jaw cue into eating behaviour

model.text: He’ll take a bit, then stop and push it away. I’m honestly not sure how much he’s drinking.
Have you noticed any swelling of his face, a hot or red cheek, a temperature, or difficulty opening his mouth or swallowing?
model.why: Screens for spreading dental infection needing same-day hospital care

model.text: I haven’t looked properly — he won’t let us near his mouth. We haven’t taken his temperature.
And the other common things — has he opened his bowels normally, any change in his wee, pulling at his ears, any falls or knocks?
model.why: Covers constipation, urinary infection, ear pain and injury

model.text: I’d have to check his charts for bowels and wee. I haven’t noticed anything with his ears, and nobody’s reported a fall.
How does Daniel usually show you he’s in pain? Some people have a particular sound or gesture.
model.why: Uses the carer’s knowledge of his pain behaviours

model.text: He goes quiet, then he gets cross. A bit like this week, now I think about it.
What’s been going through your mind about all this, and what’s worried you most?
model.why: Explores the carer’s ideas and concerns without blame

model.text: Honestly, we’re short-staffed and he’s been up every night. We thought it was behaviour. And examining him is really hard — he gets so distressed. We just want him calmer.

That sounds exhausting, and you clearly care about him — you noticed all of this. Can I share what I think? When someone who finds it hard to tell us about pain suddenly starts hitting his face, holding his jaw and not eating, the most likely explanation is that something hurts. It looks to me like his teeth or mouth — possibly an abscess.
model.why: Names the likely physical cause and gently challenges overshadowing

model.text: Oh. I didn’t think of that. I just assumed it was him.

It’s a really common assumption, and you’re not to blame. But it matters: people with a learning disability too often have pain or illness missed because it’s put down to their condition. A calming medicine wouldn’t fix a toothache — it would just make him drowsy while it carried on hurting.
model.why: Explains why sedation is wrong, supporting rather than criticising the carer

model.text: That makes sense. But how do we examine him if he won’t let anyone near him?

We adapt to him. I’ll see him in person today, at a quiet time with a longer appointment — the last slot, when the waiting room’s empty. You or whoever knows him best comes too. We go at his pace, show him what we’ll do first, and use a pain-checking tool with you. If he has a hospital passport, bring it.
model.why: Concrete reasonable adjustments rather than skipping the examination

model.text: I’ll check whether he has one and bring it if so.
Great. Daniel — we’re going to find out what’s hurting and make it better. I’ll show you everything before I do it.
model.why: Speaks to Daniel directly in simple language

model.text: In the meantime, regular paracetamol at the correct dose for his weight is fine to start now for pain, and soft food and plenty to drink. If it is his tooth, he’ll need an urgent dentist — I’ll help arrange that, and we’ll ask the dental team about adjustments too.
model.why: Treats pain now and plans definitive dental care

model.text: What if he won’t let us look even then?

Then we’ll decide together what’s in his best interests, involving you and anyone else who knows him well — that might mean a specialist dental service that can see him with extra support. The one thing we won’t do is decide it’s just behaviour without checking.
model.why: Mental Capacity Act best-interests route, with least-restrictive options

model.text: While we’re here, I’d like to check he’s on our learning disability register, record his adjustments so every visit is easier, and book his annual health check.
model.why: Uses the contact to address health inequality systematically

model.text: I don’t think he’s had one of those for a while.
Then let’s sort it. Can you tell me back what we’re doing today?
Paracetamol now, bring him in this afternoon with his passport if he has one, and probably an urgent dentist. And not just calming him.

Exactly. If his face swells, he gets a temperature, can’t open his mouth, struggles to swallow or breathe, or stops drinking, don’t wait for the appointment — ring 999 or go to A&E. If anything else worries you before then, call us straight back. Thank you for being such a good advocate for him today.
model.why: Specific red flags with clear escalation and positive reinforcement of the carer

model.text: Thanks, doctor. I’m glad I rang.

social.t: Carers under pressure may default to behavioural explanations. Recognise their effort, enlist them as expert historians, and support them to advocate.
Daniel may communicate pain through behaviour rather than words. His usual cues, routine and preferences should be recorded for every future contact.

legal.t: Services must make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. Failing to adapt the examination is a failure of this duty, not a clinical choice.

Assume capacity; support him to decide; assess decision-specifically. Without an attorney or deputy, the support worker cannot consent for him. If he lacks capacity, act in his best interests after consulting those who know him, choosing the least restrictive option.
NHS services must identify, record, flag and meet the communication needs of people with a disability.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): make sure vulnerable patients receive the same standard of care. Challenge diagnostic overshadowing kindly and document the adjustments made.
NHS England STOMP: avoid psychotropics for behaviour without a clear indication; NICE NG11 limits antipsychotic use to specific circumstances with close review.

community.h: Support for Daniel and his carers
community.t: Community learning disability team; specialist (special care) dental services for adapted dental treatment; Mencap for easy-read resources; hospital passport kept up to date.

redFlags: Facial swelling, fever, trismus, difficulty swallowing or breathing — spreading dental infection needing same-day hospital care
Not drinking or passing little urine — dehydration
Injury from self-harm, especially around the face and eyes
Any other new physical sign the carer notices, such as vomiting, abdominal distension or reduced consciousness
psychosocial: His usual routine, communication and how he shows pain
Carer fatigue and staffing pressures behind the request for sedation
Recent changes in environment or staff, considered only after physical causes
ice: Idea (carer): “It’s his autism playing up — a behaviour thing”
Concern (carer): exhausted staff and a distressing examination; Daniel cannot say what hurts
Expectation (carer): something to calm him down without examining him

playbook.diagnosis: Probable dental pain (possible abscess) presenting as behaviour change in a young man with a learning disability and autism, at risk of diagnostic overshadowing: “Hitting his face, holding his jaw and not eating most likely mean his mouth hurts.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Daniel can’t tell us in words that his tooth hurts, so he’s telling us the only way he can — by holding his jaw, hitting his face and refusing food. If we listen to that, we can fix the pain, and the behaviour usually settles with it.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re exhausted and you want him calmer — so do I. The quickest way to a calmer Daniel is to find what’s hurting and treat it.”
management.psychosocial: Support the worker rather than criticise; involve the person who knows Daniel best in the adjusted appointment; record his communication needs so future contacts are easier.
sharedPlan: Same-day face-to-face assessment with reasonable adjustments (quiet slot, longer time, familiar supporter, hospital passport, pain tool)
Analgesia now; urgent dental care, including a specialist dental service if needed; best-interests decision if he lacks capacity
No sedation; confirm learning disability register, record adjustments and book the annual health check
safetyNet: Facial swelling, fever, trismus, swallowing or breathing difficulty, or not drinking: 999 or A&E
Review after dental treatment to confirm the behaviour has settled; if not, look again for another cause

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you see the patient behind the diagnosis label. Candidates fail it by agreeing with the carer, by avoiding a difficult examination, and by leaving Daniel out of his own consultation.

items.fail: Prescribing a sedating medicine “for a few nights” to help the staff cope.
items.why: Sedating unexplained distress risks missing a treatable cause and is contrary to NICE NG11 and the STOMP programme.
items.fix: “A calming medicine wouldn’t fix a toothache. Let’s find what’s hurting.”

items.fail: Accepting “it’s his autism” without asking what his usual self looks like.
items.why: Without a baseline you cannot see the change — and the change is the diagnostic clue.
items.fix: “Tell me about Daniel on a normal week. What’s different now?”

items.fail: Missing the jaw-holding because you never asked where he was hitting himself.
items.why: The location of self-injury often points to the site of pain. Generic questions miss it.
items.fix: Ask specifically: “Where on himself is he hitting? Is he holding any part of his body?”

items.fail: Talking over Daniel for the whole consultation.
items.why: He is the patient. Examiners mark ignoring him as a Relating to Others failure.
items.fix: Greet him by name, explain simply what will happen, and speak to him again at the end.

items.fail: Telling the support worker they have been negligent.
items.why: Criticism alienates the person you need as an ally and historian; diagnostic overshadowing is a system problem.
items.fix: “It’s a really common assumption and you’re not to blame — let’s work it out together.”

items.fail: Ending with “bring him in sometime this week” and no red flags.
items.why: A possible dental abscess can spread. Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Same-day adjusted appointment, and name the 999 signs: facial swelling, fever, trismus, swallowing or breathing difficulty, not drinking.

It’s a really common assumption, and you’re not to blame. But it matters: people with a learning disability too often have pain or illness missed because it’s put down to their condition. A calming medicine wouldn’t fix a toothache — it would just make him drowsy while it carried on hurting.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains why sedation is wrong, supporting rather than criticising the carer

SCA_MODELS.text: That makes sense. But how do we examine him if he won’t let anyone near him?

We adapt to him. I’ll see him in person today, at a quiet time with a longer appointment — the last slot, when the waiting room’s empty. You or whoever knows him best comes too. We go at his pace, show him what we’ll do first, and use a pain-checking tool with you. If he has a hospital passport, bring it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Concrete reasonable adjustments rather than skipping the examination

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll check whether he has one and bring it if so.
Great. Daniel — we’re going to find out what’s hurting and make it better. I’ll show you everything before I do it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Speaks to Daniel directly in simple language

SCA_MODELS.text: In the meantime, regular paracetamol at the correct dose for his weight is fine to start now for pain, and soft food and plenty to drink. If it is his tooth, he’ll need an urgent dentist — I’ll help arrange that, and we’ll ask the dental team about adjustments too.
SCA_MODELS.why: Treats pain now and plans definitive dental care

SCA_MODELS.text: What if he won’t let us look even then?

Then we’ll decide together what’s in his best interests, involving you and anyone else who knows him well — that might mean a specialist dental service that can see him with extra support. The one thing we won’t do is decide it’s just behaviour without checking.
SCA_MODELS.why: Mental Capacity Act best-interests route, with least-restrictive options

SCA_MODELS.text: While we’re here, I’d like to check he’s on our learning disability register, record his adjustments so every visit is easier, and book his annual health check.
SCA_MODELS.why: Uses the contact to address health inequality systematically

SCA_MODELS.text: I don’t think he’s had one of those for a while.
Then let’s sort it. Can you tell me back what we’re doing today?
Paracetamol now, bring him in this afternoon with his passport if he has one, and probably an urgent dentist. And not just calming him.

Exactly. If his face swells, he gets a temperature, can’t open his mouth, struggles to swallow or breathe, or stops drinking, don’t wait for the appointment — ring 999 or go to A&E. If anything else worries you before then, call us straight back. Thank you for being such a good advocate for him today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific red flags with clear escalation and positive reinforcement of the carer

SCA_MODELS.text: Thanks, doctor. I’m glad I rang.

SCA_STEM.name: Daniel
SCA_STEM.recent: Support worker reports one week of hitting himself, eating poorly, not sleeping and increased agitation — a change from his usual pattern.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation requested by his support worker, who hopes for “something to calm him down”. Daniel is present.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: Equality Act 2010 (reasonable adjustments) · Mental Capacity Act 2005 · NICE NG11 (challenging behaviour and learning disabilities, 2015) · NHS England STOMP programme · LeDeR programme · Accessible Information Standard
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: New self-injury, poor eating and poor sleep in a young man who cannot easily report pain is a physical problem until proved otherwise. Jaw-holding points to dental pain. Assess him in person with reasonable adjustments, find and treat the cause, and do not sedate distress.

points.t: Attributing new symptoms to the learning disability or autism rather than looking for a cause. LeDeR reviews of deaths of people with a learning disability and autistic people repeatedly identify it as a contributor to avoidable harm.

NICE NG11: when behaviour that challenges develops or changes, assess for physical health problems, including pain, and consider dental problems, constipation, infection and sensory problems. Here jaw-holding plus poor eating makes dental pain or abscess the leading possibility.

NICE NG11 advises considering antipsychotic medication for behaviour that challenges only when psychological and other interventions have not helped or the risk is severe, and reviewing it closely. NHS England’s STOMP programme aims to stop inappropriate psychotropic prescribing in this group.

points.h: Reasonable adjustments are a legal duty
points.t: Equality Act 2010: longer or quieter appointments, the first or last slot, a familiar supporter present, step-by-step explanation, desensitised examination and pain-assessment tools such as DisDAT. The Accessible Information Standard requires communication needs to be recorded and met. “He hates being examined” means adapt, not omit.

Mental Capacity Act 2005: assume Daniel has capacity, give him every practicable support to decide, and assess decision-specifically. A support worker cannot consent for him. If he lacks capacity for the examination or treatment, act in his best interests, consult those who know him, and choose the least restrictive option.

People on the GP learning disability register are offered an annual health check from age 14, with a health action plan. Use this contact to check he is on the register, flag his reasonable adjustments and book the check.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Greeted Daniel directly, then used an open question about what had changed from his usual self.
Staffing pressures, sleepless nights for carers, his routine and how he usually communicates pain.
Picked up the face-hitting, jaw-holding and stopping eating, and pursued each.
The worker’s belief it was behaviour, fatigue and difficulty examining him, and the request for calming medication.
Same-day face-to-face examination with adjustments: mouth and teeth, ears, abdomen, temperature; urine if feasible; pain-assessment tool.
Dental pain or abscess first; ear or throat infection, constipation, urinary infection, injury; mood or environmental change only after physical causes.
Asked about facial swelling, fever, trismus, swallowing, breathing and fluid intake.
Probable dental pain causing behaviour change, and named diagnostic overshadowing kindly.
No sedation; analgesia now; urgent dental care with adjustments; best-interests process if he lacks capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005).
Learning disability register, reasonable adjustments recorded, hospital passport used, annual health check booked.
Same-day review; 999 or A&E for swelling, fever, trismus, swallowing or breathing difficulty, or not drinking.

social.t: Carers under pressure may default to behavioural explanations. Recognise their effort, enlist them as expert historians, and support them to advocate.
Daniel may communicate pain through behaviour rather than words. His usual cues, routine and preferences should be recorded for every future contact.

legal.t: Services must make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. Failing to adapt the examination is a failure of this duty, not a clinical choice.

Assume capacity; support him to decide; assess decision-specifically. Without an attorney or deputy, the support worker cannot consent for him. If he lacks capacity, act in his best interests after consulting those who know him, choosing the least restrictive option.
NHS services must identify, record, flag and meet the communication needs of people with a disability.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): make sure vulnerable patients receive the same standard of care. Challenge diagnostic overshadowing kindly and document the adjustments made.
NHS England STOMP: avoid psychotropics for behaviour without a clear indication; NICE NG11 limits antipsychotic use to specific circumstances with close review.

community.h: Support for Daniel and his carers
community.t: Community learning disability team; specialist (special care) dental services for adapted dental treatment; Mencap for easy-read resources; hospital passport kept up to date.

redFlags: Facial swelling, fever, trismus, difficulty swallowing or breathing — spreading dental infection needing same-day hospital care
Not drinking or passing little urine — dehydration
Injury from self-harm, especially around the face and eyes
Any other new physical sign the carer notices, such as vomiting, abdominal distension or reduced consciousness
psychosocial: His usual routine, communication and how he shows pain
Carer fatigue and staffing pressures behind the request for sedation
Recent changes in environment or staff, considered only after physical causes
ice: Idea (carer): “It’s his autism playing up — a behaviour thing”
Concern (carer): exhausted staff and a distressing examination; Daniel cannot say what hurts
Expectation (carer): something to calm him down without examining him

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Probable dental pain (possible abscess) presenting as behaviour change in a young man with a learning disability and autism, at risk of diagnostic overshadowing: “Hitting his face, holding his jaw and not eating most likely mean his mouth hurts.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Daniel can’t tell us in words that his tooth hurts, so he’s telling us the only way he can — by holding his jaw, hitting his face and refusing food. If we listen to that, we can fix the pain, and the behaviour usually settles with it.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re exhausted and you want him calmer — so do I. The quickest way to a calmer Daniel is to find what’s hurting and treat it.”
management.psychosocial: Support the worker rather than criticise; involve the person who knows Daniel best in the adjusted appointment; record his communication needs so future contacts are easier.
sharedPlan: Same-day face-to-face assessment with reasonable adjustments (quiet slot, longer time, familiar supporter, hospital passport, pain tool)
Analgesia now; urgent dental care, including a specialist dental service if needed; best-interests decision if he lacks capacity
No sedation; confirm learning disability register, record adjustments and book the annual health check
safetyNet: Facial swelling, fever, trismus, swallowing or breathing difficulty, or not drinking: 999 or A&E
Review after dental treatment to confirm the behaviour has settled; if not, look again for another cause

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you see the patient behind the diagnosis label. Candidates fail it by agreeing with the carer, by avoiding a difficult examination, and by leaving Daniel out of his own consultation.

items.fail: Prescribing a sedating medicine “for a few nights” to help the staff cope.
items.why: Sedating unexplained distress risks missing a treatable cause and is contrary to NICE NG11 and the STOMP programme.
items.fix: “A calming medicine wouldn’t fix a toothache. Let’s find what’s hurting.”

items.fail: Accepting “it’s his autism” without asking what his usual self looks like.
items.why: Without a baseline you cannot see the change — and the change is the diagnostic clue.
items.fix: “Tell me about Daniel on a normal week. What’s different now?”

items.fail: Missing the jaw-holding because you never asked where he was hitting himself.
items.why: The location of self-injury often points to the site of pain. Generic questions miss it.
items.fix: Ask specifically: “Where on himself is he hitting? Is he holding any part of his body?”

items.fail: Talking over Daniel for the whole consultation.
items.why: He is the patient. Examiners mark ignoring him as a Relating to Others failure.
items.fix: Greet him by name, explain simply what will happen, and speak to him again at the end.

items.fail: Telling the support worker they have been negligent.
items.why: Criticism alienates the person you need as an ally and historian; diagnostic overshadowing is a system problem.
items.fix: “It’s a really common assumption and you’re not to blame — let’s work it out together.”

items.fail: Ending with “bring him in sometime this week” and no red flags.
items.why: A possible dental abscess can spread. Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Same-day adjusted appointment, and name the 999 signs: facial swelling, fever, trismus, swallowing or breathing difficulty, not drinking.
